    Reading a 1D network (Deltares D-Flow FM) with pyramids-mesh¶

    Most mesh files describe a 2D surface — a sheet of triangles or quads. But hydraulic models of rivers and channels store a 1D network: nodes joined by edges, with no faces at all. This notebook reads a Deltares D-Flow FM UGRID *_net.nc file — the korte-woerden channel schematic — as a 1D network.

    Why this case is special. pyramids' built-in UGRID reader always builds a 2D Mesh2d, whatever topology dimension a file declares — so MeshDataset.read_file on a pure-1D file fails (it looks for a face table that is not there). The network is read through the deltares1d driver instead: Mesh1d.read_file(path, driver="deltares1d") parses the UGRID mesh1d topology — the node coordinates and the edge-node table — straight into a Mesh1d, with no manual array handling.

    2. Imports¶

    We import Mesh1d and MeshDataset. The split matters here: a 2D driver hands back a MeshDataset (which wraps a Mesh2d), but a 1D network is read with Mesh1d.read_file and comes back as a bare Mesh1d — which is exactly what this notebook does. Importing from pyramids also puts its vendored GDAL/PROJ data in place for you, so nothing about it is order-sensitive in a notebook — just import the names you use.

    In [1]:
    Copied! 
    from pyramids.netcdf.ugrid import Mesh1d, MeshDataset
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    from pyramids.netcdf.ugrid import Mesh1d, MeshDataset from pathlib import Path import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

    3. Locate the data¶

    The Deltares folder holds several UGRID samples. We use the pure-1D korte-woerden-1d_FlowFM_net.nc (network topology, no results).

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    DATA = Path("../../examples/data")
net_file = DATA / "deltares1d" / "korte-woerden-1d_FlowFM_net.nc"
net_file.name, net_file.exists()
    DATA = Path("../../examples/data") net_file = DATA / "deltares1d" / "korte-woerden-1d_FlowFM_net.nc" net_file.name, net_file.exists()
    Out[2]:
    ('korte-woerden-1d_FlowFM_net.nc', True)

    4. Why MeshDataset.read_file refuses¶

    Pointing MeshDataset.read_file at a 1D file raises — the reader tries to build a 2D mesh and finds no face table. We catch it so the notebook keeps running.

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    try:
    MeshDataset.read_file(net_file)
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, "->", e)
    try: MeshDataset.read_file(net_file) except Exception as e: print(type(e).__name__, "->", e)
    ValueError -> Cannot read face_node_connectivity for mesh 'network'.

    5. Read the network¶

    Mesh1d.read_file with driver="deltares1d" reads the 1D discretisation directly — nodes, edge connectivity, CRS — all through the pyramids GDAL substrate, with no external libraries.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    net = Mesh1d.read_file(net_file, driver="deltares1d")
{"n_node": net.n_node, "n_edge": net.n_edge,
 "epsg": net.crs,
 "bounds": tuple(round(b, 1) for b in net.bounds)}
    net = Mesh1d.read_file(net_file, driver="deltares1d") {"n_node": net.n_node, "n_edge": net.n_edge, "epsg": net.crs, "bounds": tuple(round(b, 1) for b in net.bounds)}

    86 nodes, 91 edges, EPSG 28992 (Amersfoort / RD New, metres). The bounds span ~320 m x ~685 m;

    more edges than nodes means the network contains loops (not a simple tree).

    Edge lengths, on the other hand, are a natural graph property. We summarise the 91 edge lengths (metres, since the CRS is projected):

    In [6]:
    Copied! 
    import pandas as pd
L = net.edge_lengths
pd.Series(L).describe().round(2).to_frame("edge_length_m")
    import pandas as pd L = net.edge_lengths pd.Series(L).describe().round(2).to_frame("edge_length_m")

    91 edges, lengths from a fraction of a metre up to ~218 m, averaging ~30 m — typical for a channel broken into computational segments.

    7. Draw the network by hand¶

    A Mesh1d has no plot() of its own, so we draw it as a graph: loop the edge table, draw each edge as a line segment between its two node coordinates, then scatter the nodes on top. Equal aspect keeps the geometry true (the CRS is in metres).

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    from matplotlib.collections import LineCollection
from cleopatra.basemap.tiles import add_tiles

node_x, node_y = net.node_x, net.node_y
enc = net.edge_node_connectivity.data
segments = [[(node_x[a], node_y[a]), (node_x[b], node_y[b])] for a, b in enc]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 9))
lc = LineCollection(segments, colors="#1a6faf", linewidths=2.0, alpha=0.9, zorder=2)
ax.add_collection(lc)
ax.plot(node_x, node_y, "o", color="white", ms=5, mec="#1a6faf", mew=1.2, zorder=3)
pad = 30
ax.set_xlim(node_x.min() - pad, node_x.max() + pad)
ax.set_ylim(node_y.min() - pad, node_y.max() + pad)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_title("korte-woerden — 1D channel network", fontsize=11, pad=8)
ax.axis("off")
add_tiles(ax, crs=28992, alpha=0.55)
    from matplotlib.collections import LineCollection from cleopatra.basemap.tiles import add_tiles node_x, node_y = net.node_x, net.node_y enc = net.edge_node_connectivity.data segments = [[(node_x[a], node_y[a]), (node_x[b], node_y[b])] for a, b in enc] fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 9)) lc = LineCollection(segments, colors="#1a6faf", linewidths=2.0, alpha=0.9, zorder=2) ax.add_collection(lc) ax.plot(node_x, node_y, "o", color="white", ms=5, mec="#1a6faf", mew=1.2, zorder=3) pad = 30 ax.set_xlim(node_x.min() - pad, node_x.max() + pad) ax.set_ylim(node_y.min() - pad, node_y.max() + pad) ax.set_aspect("equal") ax.set_title("korte-woerden — 1D channel network", fontsize=11, pad=8) ax.axis("off") add_tiles(ax, crs=28992, alpha=0.55)
    Out[7]:
    <Axes: title={'center': 'korte-woerden — 1D channel network'}>

    That is the channel schematic: a branching, partly looped network of reaches. Each red dot is a network node; each blue segment is an edge the solver routes flow along.

    8. The network as vectors¶

    to_geodataframe() turns the network into a geopandas GeoDataFrame — one LineString per edge (location="edge") or one Point per node (location="node"), CRS-stamped from the network. That is the bridge to the whole vector-GIS ecosystem: spatial joins, export to shapefile/GeoPackage, overlay with other layers.

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    gdf_edges = net.to_geodataframe(location="edge")
gdf_edges.head()
    gdf_edges = net.to_geodataframe(location="edge") gdf_edges.head()

    Takeaway¶

    A 1D network is a graph, not a surface. pyramids keeps it in a dedicated Mesh1d class, and the deltares1d driver reads a D-Flow FM UGRID .nc straight into it — Mesh1d.read_file(path, driver="deltares1d") — with no manual array parsing. From there you get edge lengths, bounds, nearest-neighbour trees, a GeoDataFrame of lines or points, and — for a directed network — topological ordering. There are no faces, areas or centroids, and that is correct: a channel network has none.
